where: quiz Q7, together with the Section 2 sentence "ARM Cortex-M, from Unit 2, gives the CPU two privilege levels"
problem: Cortex-M0 and Cortex-M0+ implement ARMv6-M. In ARMv6-M the CONTROL register has bit 1 (SPSEL) but no bit 0 (nPRIV), so thread mode is always privileged and no unprivileged state exists. Unprivileged thread mode comes with ARMv7-M and ARMv8-M cores (Cortex-M3, M4, M7, M23, M33). A Cortex-M0+ therefore cannot run a user/kernel split at all, and the "yes" answer to Q7 has no valid basis.
fix: Say in Section 2 that only cores implementing nPRIV (ARMv7-M, ARMv8-M) give two privilege levels. Reword Q7: "An RTOS that has a user/kernel split runs on a Cortex-M3 (or M4) with no MPU and no MMU. Does the split still buy anything?" Answer unchanged: yes for instructions (interrupt controller, PRIMASK, MSP stay out of reach), no for memory.

where: Section 1, last paragraph ("Firmware and OS run privileged in kernel space; the application runs unprivileged in user space")
problem: Written as a universal fact. The split is a build option, and most small RTOS builds, including the default FreeRTOS Cortex-M demos, run every task privileged inside the kernel image.
fix: "In a build that enables the split, firmware and OS run privileged in kernel space and the application runs unprivileged in user space. Without that option every task runs privileged too, and the protection described in Section 3 is absent."

problem: "You meet this design in every RTOS" is too strong, and "FreeRTOS calls it kernel and user modes" is not FreeRTOS terminology: FreeRTOS speaks of the kernel and of tasks, and only its ARMv7-M MPU port offers unprivileged tasks.
fix: "Many RTOSes offer this design. FreeRTOS's ARMv7-M MPU port lets tasks run unprivileged against a privileged kernel; Linux calls the two sides kernel space and user space."

where: Section 2 ("cannot change the stack pointer") and quiz Q7 answer
problem: Unprivileged code changes its own stack pointer constantly: ordinary pushes, pops and locals all move the PSP. What it cannot do is switch CONTROL.SPSEL to the MSP, or read and write MSP/PSP with MSR and MRS.
fix: "...cannot mask interrupts, cannot reach the interrupt controller, cannot select or write the main stack pointer, and cannot reach registers the MPU has fenced off." Use the same wording in the Q7 answer.

problem: "Each call costs one change down and one up" reverses the directions used in Worked example 1, where entering the kernel is counted as a change up and the exception return as a change down. A student copying the answer writes the wrong direction.
fix: "Each call costs one privilege change up (into the kernel) and one change down (back to the task), so 2 x 3 = 6 privilege changes."
